title: Gemini 4 Argon for CAD: Can It Rebuild a Part From a Drawing?
summary: Gemini 4 Argon led CAD Arena on 65 scored trials. Follow a slotted bracket from a supplier drawing to an editable AutoCAD block or Revit family.
body_markdown:
A mounting bracket can look right from the front even when the slots run the wrong way. The mistake shows up when someone tries to slide the equipment into position. For a drafter working from a supplier PDF, that makes a better test of an AI model than asking it to draw a convincing piece of metal. Can it follow the views well enough to put each feature where it belongs? And can the next person change the part?


Gemini 4 Argon, which Google previewed on September 30 and released more broadly on October 13, has been tested on exactly that kind of drawing-to-CAD work. Google made Argon available through its paid Gemini API and to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app.[Google’s initial announcement](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/) and[October release](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/)


## How Gemini 4 Argon scored on CAD Arena


Normal’s CAD Arena starts with engineering drawings for 18 mechanical parts. Each model gets a chance to rebuild each part in five CAD systems, for 90 trials. The evaluator checks both the shape and how editable the result is. On the all-platform leaderboard, Argon posted the highest mean score, **0.754 out of 1 across 65 scored trials** . The other 25 trials produced no scored output. In Autodesk Fusion specifically, none of Argon’s trials produced a usable result.[Normal’s CAD Arena results and scoring rules](https://normal.ai/leaderboard/cad-arena)


Both numbers matter if you run a drafting team. The 0.754 tells you something about the files Argon produced. The 65 tells you how often the evaluator had a file it could score. And if your team uses AutoCAD, there’s another detail worth catching before you choose a tool. The Autodesk application in the test was Fusion. A DWG with your blocks and layers asks something different of the software.


## Gemini 4 Argon for CAD drawing interpretation


Take the bracket back to the supplier sheet. Its front view gives the spacing between the round holes. The top view shows the direction of the slots. A section tells you the plate thickness. Those three pieces of information will eventually live in one object, but they’re easier to check while each one still has an address on the drawing.


> Read this bracket drawing and give me the hole spacing, slot length and direction, and plate thickness. Beside each value, identify the view and dimension you used. Leave an unmarked dimension open.


Suppose the reply gives a 30 mm slot length. Zoom in on the dimension’s arrowheads. If they land on the centers of the rounded ends, 30 mm is the distance between centers. The overall length also includes the slot width. That one check determines which value belongs in the block or family.


## Carry the bracket into AutoCAD or Revit with ArchiLabs Desktop


With the dimensions settled, an AutoCAD drafter might need a reusable detail block. A Revit team might need a family whose mounting centers can change when the equipment changes. Give ArchiLabs Desktop the supplier PDF and the checked dimensions, tell it which of those deliverables you need, and identify the insertion point your team uses. Desktop can create and edit native Revit elements and AutoCAD drawing objects.[Explore ArchiLabs Desktop](https://archilabs.ai/desktop)


For a first review, change the mounting-center spacing. If the holes move together as intended and the outside edges stay put, the next equipment revision has somewhere to go. That's a more revealing handoff than a screenshot of the bracket at its original size.
